title: Who is pro-AI, against, or neutral in the 2026 midterms?

methodology.summary: Each candidate carries one coarse AI stance tag — pro, against, or neutral — coded from cited public campaign statements and legislative records. The tag is a reading of the public record, not a score of how dangerous the person is, and not an endorsement.

stances.pro: Public record favors accelerating AI deployment, data-center buildout, faster permitting, or opposing broad new federal AI rules.
stances.against: Public record favors construction pauses, extensive new federal AI rules, public control of advanced systems, or making AI crackdown a central campaign plank.
stances.neutral: AI-specific record is thin, mixed across dimensions, or still unscored on the main AI governance questions.

methodology.sources_note: Primary evidence set is AI Congress race pages (aicongress.us), plus named news interviews when a campaign statement is quoted there. Missing evidence is marked, never filled in.

candidates.name: Jon Ossoff
candidates.summary: Treats AI as economically useful while calling for binding safeguards on high-consequence uses and for data centres to pay their own grid costs.

evidence.quote: My office is investigating AI data centers' impact on rising power bills.

candidates.name: Mike Collins
candidates.summary: Favors faster permitting, expanded energy supply, and business-led growth; AI-specific governance questions stay thin in the public record.

evidence.quote: Highlights the PERMIT Act and an all-of-the-above energy agenda to lower costs and spur growth.

candidates.name: Ashley Hinson
candidates.summary: Supports rapid AI adoption, rural data-centre investment, workforce prep, and China-focused export enforcement while opposing broad regulation.

evidence.quote: Supports AI leadership and rural data-center investment while rejecting heavy regulation.

candidates.name: Josh Turek
candidates.summary: Worker, training, and antimonopoly platform is detailed; a dedicated AI or data-centre plan is not in the public record used here.

evidence.quote: Campaign has not released a dedicated AI or data-center plan.

candidates.name: Abdul El-Sayed
candidates.summary: Calls for national AI guardrails, democratic control of advanced systems, and an FDA-style overseer for model development.

evidence.quote: We need AI under democracy and AI under control… an SCC or FDA-style regulatory agency.
evidence.source: CBS News Detroit / Detroit Economic Club

candidates.name: Mike Rogers
candidates.summary: Supports a temporary Michigan construction pause and ratepayer protections while still framing AI investment and jobs as strategic priorities.

evidence.quote: Supports a temporary Michigan pause and ratepayer protections while emphasizing AI-related investment and competitiveness.

candidates.name: James Talarico
candidates.summary: Presses tighter conditions on AI infrastructure and data-centre buildout relative to a market-led energy and technology posture.

evidence.quote: Contrasts tighter infrastructure conditions with a more market-led energy and technology posture.

candidates.name: Ken Paxton
candidates.summary: Favors a more market-led energy and technology posture on data centres, while also carrying a narrower record of suits and rules aimed at platforms and AI bots.

evidence.quote: Market-led energy and technology posture on the AI Congress Texas scorecard.
Has pitched lawsuits against major social platforms and restrictions on AI bots interacting with underage users.

candidates.name: Roy Cooper
candidates.summary: Addresses energy affordability with a tighter approach to data-centre expansion than a pure national AI-competition frame.

evidence.quote: Both candidates address energy affordability, while taking different approaches to data-center expansion and national AI competition.

candidates.name: Michael Whatley
candidates.summary: Frames data-centre expansion inside a national AI competition and growth posture relative to Cooper’s affordability-first line.

evidence.quote: Different approaches to data-center expansion and national AI competition.

candidates.name: Troy Jackson
candidates.summary: Proposes stronger cost and labor conditions on AI-related infrastructure relative to case-by-case development.

evidence.quote: Jackson proposes stronger cost and labor conditions, while Collins favors case-by-case development and public computing investment.

candidates.name: Susan Collins
candidates.summary: Favors case-by-case development and public computing investment rather than a single accelerate-or-pause line.

evidence.quote: Favors case-by-case development and public computing investment.

candidates.name: Sherrod Brown
candidates.summary: Makes data-centre construction and household power bills central; positions refine toward tighter conditions on large AI loads.

evidence.quote: Data-center construction and household power bills are already central to the contest.

candidates.name: Jon Husted
candidates.summary: Refines a growth-and-energy posture on data centres against an affordability-first Democratic frame.

evidence.quote: Both candidates are refining positions as data-center construction and power bills sit at the centre of the race.
